summary: For ages 7–9, teach that fossils reveal ancient ENVIRONMENTS, not just ancient animals: marine fossils (shells, ammonites, corals) found inland or high on a mountain show the area was once sea, and plant fossils (ferns, palms vs. desert plants) show whether a place was warm/wet forest, swamp, or dry. The core move is child-friendly uniformitarian inference — 'this kind of organism (or, for extinct ones like ammonites, its closest living relatives) lives in ___ today, so long ago here was ___' — paired with the big idea that places change dramatically over deep time (a seabed became a mountaintop; Antarctica once had forests). The reconstruction/detective activity is the primary vehicle; matching and diagnostic tasks check the inference and guard against the 'animals were carried/washed up' and 'the place was always like this' misconceptions.
misconceptions: 'Sea fossils on land mean the sea animal walked/was carried onto land' — the area itself was once under the sea and has since risen.
'The environment was always like it is now' — fossils show places change dramatically (seabed → mountain; forest → ice).
'Fossils only tell us about the animal' — they also indicate climate and habitat via where such organisms live.
'A single odd fossil proves a whole environment' — scientists look for consistent assemblages of fossils.
'Plant fossils aren't useful evidence' — plants are strong indicators of past temperature and moisture.

activities.title: Reconstruct the past from fossil clues
steps: See a map pin showing that marine fossils have been found far inland and high up on a mountain, which sets up the puzzle: how did sea creatures end up there?
Examine a present-day scene, e.g. a windswept mountaintop or a dry, dusty hill.

Collect the fossil clues scattered in that scene's rock (on the mountaintop, e.g. a sea shell, a coiled ammonite and a coral; on the dry hill, e.g. a fern and a palm frond) and place each onto an evidence tray.

For each clue, answer the question 'where does this kind of organism, or its closest living relatives, live today?' (sea shells and corals → the sea; ammonites are extinct, but their relatives such as the nautilus and squid live in the sea; ferns → mostly damp places; palms → warm places).
Once the clues agree, trigger the scene to transform: the mountaintop becomes a warm shallow sea full of ammonites, or the dry hill becomes a steamy fern forest — right where the learner is standing.
Read or state the 'why?' reasoning aloud: 'These lived in the sea, so this place was once sea.'
Take a twist round with mixed-up or insufficient clues and decide to WAIT until the evidence points one way before reconstructing.
activities.insight: A past environment can be reconstructed from fossil clues by matching each organism, or its closest living relatives, to where they live today; when the clues agree they reveal that a place changed beyond recognition over deep time, and the fossils are the evidence.

activities.title: Then vs. now: flip the landscape
steps: View a modern scene (a mountaintop) and flip or slide it to reveal its ancient version (a shallow sea).
Tap a fossil in the scene to reveal the reasoning caption: 'this lived in the sea → here was once sea.'
Say in your own words what the fossil tells you about the place long ago.
activities.insight: The same spot can look completely different now and in the deep past, and a fossil clue justifies the change from 'mountaintop today' to 'ancient shallow sea.'

activities.title: Match the clue to the ancient environment
steps: Match each fossil to the past environment it indicates: coral and ammonite → sea; fern and palm → warm, wet forest; specific desert/swamp plants → desert or swamp.
Answer a question about the classic case: 'Marine fossils found on a mountain mean that place was once...?' and justify the answer (once covered by sea).
Explain why a single odd fossil is weaker evidence than several fossils that agree.
activities.insight: Fossil type maps to past environment, and consistent clues let you reason confidently from organism to habitat and climate.

activities.title: The geologist's question: reason it out and confront the flood idea
steps: Respond to a diagnostic prompt: 'A hiker finds fossils of sea shells and fish at the very top of a tall mountain. How did sea creatures end up on top of a mountain? Explain what this tells us about that place long ago.'
Explain the difference between an animal moving to a new place and the place itself changing over time.
Describe how ground that is now high up could once have been at the bottom of the sea (it was low and covered by sea long ago, then the land was pushed up very slowly over vast time).
Apply the idea to a new case: 'If you found fossils of ferns and swampy plants in a desert today, what would that tell you?'
Discuss the real example that Antarctica, now ice-covered, once had temperate forests and dinosaurs — its plant fossils show environments change over deep time.
activities.insight: Sea fossils on a mountain mean the area itself was once a sea floor that was later slowly pushed up — the organisms did not climb or get washed up; the same reasoning generalises to other fossils and places, and even whole continents have changed.

checkQuestion: A hiker finds fossils of sea shells and fish at the very top of a tall mountain. How did sea creatures end up on top of a mountain? Explain what this tells us about that place long ago.
checkAnswer: That place was once under the sea — it was a sea floor long ago. The rock later became a mountain (the land was pushed up over vast time), or the sea once covered the area. The fossils show the environment was once a sea; the animals didn't travel up the mountain.
